title: Chapter 48: The Man Who Cannot Read, Part 2 of 5: Before Dawn
html:
Corin did not sleep.
He lay on his bench under the skulls with the Ledger on his chest and listened to Oren breathe on the floor below him. Slow. Deep. The breath of a man who has spent everything and is getting a little of it back, in the dark, the way a spring fills up a well. And on the other side of the vault, Lyra, on her pile of sacks by the wall, not breathing like that at all. Breathing like somebody lying very still with her eyes open.
He thought about the gray-cap boy behind the yew.
He thought about a crypt with one door and fifty-one children in it who could not walk.
He thought about a shop window full of gold dust and a tall thin woman sitting against a wall with her eyes closed, and a man on a stair with a club, and the two-note whistle, up and then down, like a man calling a dog he was fond of.
And he thought about tomorrow.
The doctor came back at the fourth bell. Corin heard him come down the three stone steps, slowly, and stop at the bottom, and stand there for a while, the way a man stands when he has come home very tired and is not sure, for a moment, which way to go. Then the long legs came down the hall between the pallets, past the braziers, and the tall stooped shape stood in the arch of the vault with the lamp in its hand and looked down at Oren asleep on the floor, and at Corin awake on the bench.
"Well," said Silas, very low. "Still alive. Both of you."
"Where were you?"
"Church Lane. The Pellow baby. Croup. She'll live." Silas put the lamp down on the floor. He sat down on the end of the bench, by Corin's stiff leg, with a crack from his knees, and took off his spectacles and rubbed his eyes. "And then the Fish Stairs."
Corin waited.
"I went down to look," said Silas. "In the dark. On my way back. I wanted to see what they'd done." He put his spectacles back on, crooked. "They've built a stage."
"A stage?"
"A platform. Boards on trestles. At the top of the Fish Stairs, where the market is, under the old fish hall roof. With red cloth nailed round the edge of it. And two braziers, one at each end, already lit, and a man in a brown coat sitting between them on a stool, keeping them going all night." Silas looked at the floor. "So that the Under-Secretary won't be cold, I suppose, when he comes at the eighth bell to give the children of the parish their sweets."
The vault was very quiet.
"All the children of the parish are to attend," said Corin. "The notice said. Are to attend."
"Yes."
"What happens to the ones who don't?"
Silas did not answer for a moment.
"Their names are written down," he said at last. "By the man in the brown coat. In a book. As children who were not brought. And then, some weeks later, a man from the Health calls at the house, very kindly, to ask after the child's health. And brings a bag of sweets." He looked at Corin. "That's how it worked last winter, in the parish of Saint Clement's. Before it came here."
"Then they'll all go."
"They'll all go. Their mothers will take them. Most of the mothers in the Lower Docks can't read the notice. But they know what in person means, and what are to attend means, and what the Health means." Silas spread his long hands on his knees. "They'll stand in the snow in a line with their children, the way they stand in line outside the Bank, and the children will go up the steps to the stage one at a time, and a kind old man with white hair and gold spectacles will give each one a sweet out of a round silver box, and pat them on the head. And they'll eat it. There, in front of him. Because they're children, and it's a sweet." He stopped. "And next Friday the cart will come."
Corin lay on his bench.
"Can you stop it?" he said.
"No."
"Can anybody?"
"Not today." Silas looked at the floor. "Not with a hundred mothers in a line and the Watch at the bottom of the Stairs and the Health's men on the stage. If I stand up in front of that crowd and say don't eat the sweets, they'll take me away before I've finished saying it. And then there'll be nobody down here at all."
Corin was quiet for a long time.
Then he said: "They don't have to eat them."
Silas looked at him.
"They have to take them," said Corin. "They have to go up the steps and be given one and be patted on the head and have their name written in the book as a child who came. That's all the notice says. Sweets will be given. It doesn't say eaten." He looked up at the roof. "Children put sweets in their pockets all the time. To save them. To give to a brother. To eat later, in bed, so nobody can take it off them."
"And then?"
"And then they give them to their mothers. And their mothers give them to the step women. And the step women give them to you." Corin turned his head and looked at the doctor. "A hundred sweets, with the Under-Secretary's grayroot in them, given out in public, in front of the whole parish, under a notice with the Office of Public Health's seal on it. Kept, and counted, and wrapped. And taken to somebody who can test them."
Silas looked at him for a long time over his crooked spectacles.
"The step women," he said slowly.
"Juno can be at Mrs. Marta's by the fifth bell. Mrs. Marta can have the word on every step in the Lower Docks by the seventh. The landlady says the rent is late." Corin's mouth went down at the left corner. "Something like that. Mrs. Marta will know how to say it. The step women have a way of saying everything."
"And if one child eats it anyway?"
"Then one child eats it." Corin did not look away. "And not a hundred."
Silas was quiet.
Then he nodded, slowly, and stood up, and went to the far wall of the vault, where Juno was asleep on the floor in a heap of Mrs. Fitch's shawls with her cap over her face. And knelt down beside her, very gently, with a crack from his knees, and put his long hand on her shoulder.
"Juno," he said.
Juno woke at once, the way children of the Lower Docks always woke, all at once and completely, with her eyes open before her cap was off her face.
Silas told her.
She listened. She nodded. She got up off the floor, on the sides of her feet, with the small sound through her teeth, and put her cap on and pulled it down, and went to the arch.
Then she stopped, and turned round, and looked at Corin on his bench.
"And you?" she said. "What are you going to do?"
"Go and look at him," said Corin.
Juno stared at him. So did Silas.
"I've seen him once," said Corin. "Pallister. Through a knothole in a broom-cupboard door under the Bourse, for as long as it takes a man to give a woman two peppermints. And then his face in a carriage window, going past in the dark in Cinder Lane." He put his gray hand flat on the Ledger. "I've got a page on him. Lyra's written in it. Silas has written in it. His stick, his knee, his gold spectacles. But I've never stood in front of him in daylight and watched what he does with his hands. And I'd like to." He looked at the doctor. "Before Midwinter. Before I have to walk past him in a waiter's coat with a tray. I'd like to know his face properly, so that when I see it I'm not afraid of it."
"You can't walk," said Silas.
"No," said Corin. "But you've got a barrow. And a card that says fever."
The Fish Stairs
The Fish Stairs went down from the bottom of Fish Street to the river in one long wide flight of old gray stone, forty steps from top to bottom, as wide as a street. At the top was the fish hall. At the bottom was the water.
Corin had been there a hundred times. He knew it the way he knew most of the Lower Docks, from the Ledger and from his feet, half and half. He knew that the fish boats came in at the bottom of the Stairs before dawn every day but Sunday, and tied up at the iron rings in the river wall, and the fishwives went down the steps in their black shawls and their wooden clogs with their baskets on their hips and came back up with the baskets full and shining and dripping. He knew that the gulls sat on the roof of the fish hall in long white rows and screamed at everything. He knew that the steps were always wet, and in winter always iced, and that every winter somebody fell on them and broke something.
He had never seen them like this.
Silas stopped the barrow at the top of Fish Street, at the corner, under the overhang of a chandler's shop with its shutters still up, where there was a little space out of the falling snow. And Corin, lying on his back on the sacks in the bottom of the barrow with the gray blanket up to his chin and the white card that said FEVER tied to the end by his boots, turned his head on the folded sack under it, and looked.
The fish hall stood across the top of the Stairs like a great open shed. It was very old. A long roof of black timber, with the snow lying thick on it and the gulls standing in the snow, on a double row of thick iron columns, painted green once and gone to rust. No walls. Only the roof and the columns, and under them, on the stone floor, the long wooden tables where the fish were sold, scrubbed white and empty today.
And in the middle of the fish hall, between the tables, facing the top of the Stairs, the stage.
It was not big. Boards on trestles, as Silas had said, a little higher than a man's waist, with three wooden steps up to it at the front. But somebody had taken trouble with it. A cloth of red baize was nailed all round the edge, hanging to the floor, so that you could not see the trestles underneath. There was a chair on it. Not a stool. A real chair, of dark wood, with arms and a high back and a red cushion. And on either side of the chair, an iron brazier on three legs, burning bright, with the heat going up off them in a wavering haze and the snow hissing and vanishing above them before it could land.
And beside the chair, a little table. With a white cloth on it. And on the white cloth, a box.
Round. Silver. The size of a cake. With the lamplight from the braziers moving on its lid.
Corin looked at it for a long time.
Then he looked at the line.
It went down the Stairs. From the foot of the three wooden steps of the stage, across the fish hall floor between the empty tables, out to the top of the Stairs, and down. All the way down. Forty steps. And along the river wall at the bottom, toward the bridges, as far as he could see in the snow. A long dark line of people, standing two and three abreast, very close together for the warmth, with the snow falling on them.
Women, mostly. In shawls. In black and brown and gray. With their heads bent. And at their skirts, holding on, children.
Small ones. Some so small they were carried. Some old enough to stand on their own, in boots too big or too small, or rags tied round their feet, stamping, hopping from one foot to the other in the snow the way children do when they are cold and have been told to stand still. Some of them crying. Most of them not. Most of them only standing, holding on to a skirt, looking up the Stairs at the fish hall, at the red cloth, at the braziers burning. At the silver box.
He could not count them. There were too many. He tried. He got to nine, and it went soft, and slid away, and he could not get it back. He lay in the barrow and looked at the long dark line going down the Stairs and along the river in the snow, and could not count it, and felt something in his chest go tight.
"Two hundred," said Silas, beside the barrow, very low. "Perhaps more. The whole parish. And Saint Clement's. I see faces from Saint Clement's."
At the bottom of the Stairs, by the river wall, there were constables. Four of them, in the Watch's blue coats and tall hats, with their rattles on their belts and their staves in their hands, standing about in the snow, stamping their feet, talking to each other, not looking at the line. And at the top, by the stage, there were other men. Not in blue. In brown. Long brown coats, belted, and brown hats, and on the breast of each coat a small badge, a round one, that caught the light. Blue enamel. Corin knew it. He had seen it on a carriage door in Cinder Lane, and on a printed label on a bag of vials, under the Bourse. The Office of Public Health.
There were six of the brown men. They stood about the stage in a loose ring. One of them, at the foot of the three wooden steps, had a stool and a high narrow desk, the kind a clerk stands at, and a great ledger open on it, and a pen. The man who had kept the braziers going all night, Corin thought. He was writing now. The woman at the head of the line had come up to the desk with a little boy in a red woolen cap, and the man in brown was asking her something, and writing down the answer.
The name. The street. The age.
Corin watched him write it.
Then he looked along the line again. Slowly. Face by face. And this time he was not trying to count. He was looking for something.
He found it at once.
It was in the hands. The children's hands. Not all of them. Not even most. But here and there, all along the line, all the way down the Stairs, a child would be standing with one hand holding its mother's skirt and the other hand in its pocket. Pushed down deep into its coat pocket, or the pocket of its pinafore, and kept there. And the mother's hand on its shoulder, not moving. Pressing. The way you press on the shoulder of a child to remind it of something it has been told.
And here and there along the line, among the black shawls and the brown ones, there were women who did not have children with them at all. Big women, mostly. Broad as doors. In shawls and men's boots, with buckets. Standing in the line as if they were waiting to be given something too. And bending down, now and then, to say a word to the child in front of them, or the child behind. Low. Quick. And straightening up again.
The step women.
He saw Bridie Kane. Halfway down the Stairs, in her brown shawl, with her bucket in her hand and her wide red face turned up toward the stage. Her eyes were red. She was not looking at the stage. She was looking at the child in front of her, a girl of about five in a gray cap, and her lips were moving.
Corin did not need to hear the words. He could see them.
In your pocket, lovey. In your pocket, and keep it there. For later. For a treat.
He let out his breath.
And at the very bottom of the Stairs, where the line turned along the river wall, small, standing a little apart from the others with her back to the wall, a girl in a cap with no mother and no child. Standing on the sides of her feet.
Juno.
She was not looking at the stage either. She was looking up the Stairs, the whole length of them, through the snow, at the corner of Fish Street. At the chandler's shop. At the barrow under the overhang, with the white card tied to the end of it.
She lifted one hand. Not a wave. Only her hand, open, for a moment, against her chest, the way you show somebody across a room that you have something.
Then she put it back in her coat.
And from up the hill behind them, along Fish Street, through the snow, came the sound of a carriage. Wheels in the soft snow, hissing. Harness creaking. And horses. Two of them. Walking, slowly, the way you walk horses when the person in the carriage is old and does not like to be shaken.
The brown men round the stage straightened up.
The constables at the bottom of the Stairs stopped talking and turned round.
And all along the line, two hundred faces, more, lifted. Down the Stairs. Along the river. Up toward the fish hall.
The carriage came down Fish Street past the chandler's shop. Past the barrow, so close that Corin could have put out his gray hand from under the blanket and touched its wheel. A plain dark carriage, well kept, with the blinds up. And on its door, a small round badge, painted. Blue.
And in its window, as it went by, a face.
An old man's face. Thin. Pink. Kind. With white hair, very fine, combed back from a high forehead. Gold spectacles. A small soft smile.
The face looked out of the window as the carriage passed the chandler's shop, at the snow, at the street, at the long line of children going down the Stairs. And it smiled a little more.
And then, just for a moment, before the carriage had quite gone by, it looked down. At the barrow under the overhang. At the white card tied to the end of it, by the boots.
FEVER.
The smile did not change at all.
Mr. Peppermint
The carriage stopped at the edge of the fish hall, and one of the brown men opened the door, and let down the step, and held up his arm.
And the Under-Secretary of the Office of Public Health got out.
He did it slowly. He was not a young man. He put out one hand, in a gray glove, and took the brown man's arm, and leaned on it, and came down the step with his left leg held out a little stiffly in front of him, the knee not bending quite as a knee should. Corin watched that knee. He knew about knees now. And in his other hand, a stick. Ebony, black and shining, as tall as his hip, with a silver head on it, the size of a child's fist, that caught the light of the braziers. A flower. A closed flower, a bud, its silver petals folded tight.
He stood on the stones of the fish hall floor and looked about him.
He was thin. Thinner than Corin had thought, from the knothole. Narrow-shouldered, in a long dark-gray coat with a collar of soft gray fur, very fine. Not tall. Not short. A small, neat, upright old man, the kind you see in the front pew of a church, or at the end of a long table at a wedding, smiling at the bride. White hair, fine as thistledown, combed back. Gold spectacles. Pink cheeks, pinker in the cold. And the face. A long gentle face, all its lines going upward, toward the eyes, the way the lines go on a face that has spent a lifetime smiling.
He smiled now. At the line. At the children. At the snow.
"Well," he said.
He did not say it loudly. But the fish hall was very quiet, and the snow was falling, and it carried. A soft voice. Warm. A little dry, like the rustle of tissue paper. The kind of voice that tells you a story when you cannot sleep.
"Well, well. What a crowd. What a great many of you. And in all this snow." He looked down the Stairs, and shook his head, smiling, as if they were all being very silly, and he was very fond of them for it. "You must be frozen, every one. We'd better be quick, hadn't we, and get you all home to your fires."
He went to the stage.
It took him a long time to get up the three wooden steps. The brown man helped him. One step, and the stiff left leg after it. And the next. At the top, he stood for a moment, getting his breath, with both hands on the silver head of his stick. Then he lowered himself into the high-backed chair with the red cushion, between the two braziers, slowly, with a small sigh, the way an old man sits down in his own chair by his own fire at the end of the day. And laid the stick across his knees.
And reached out, and picked up the round silver box from the little table at his side, and held it in his lap. And opened the lid.
Corin could not see inside it, from the corner of Fish Street. He did not need to.
He had read it in the Ledger, in Lyra's hand. Mr. Peppermint. Every Midwinter at Crown Walk. On the stairs. A round silver box. Coin tricks. Ro and I sat on the bottom step and waited for him.
"There," said Pallister. "Now. Who's first?"
The little boy in the red woolen cap was first.
His mother brought him up the three steps. She did not go up with him. She stood at the bottom with her hands twisted together in her shawl. The little boy went up on his own, slowly, holding the rail, in boots too big for him, and stood in front of the chair, between the braziers, and looked up.
Pallister leaned forward.
He did not give him the sweet at once. He looked at him. Kindly. For a long moment. He put out one gray-gloved hand and took the little boy's chin in it, very gently, and turned his face a little to the light. The way a doctor looks at a child's face. The way Silas had looked at Polly. And the little boy stood very still and let him.
Then Pallister reached behind the little boy's ear and took out a copper penny.
The boy's mouth fell open.
Pallister laughed, softly, and held the penny up so that the braziers caught it, and turned it over in his fingers, and it was gone. And he showed the boy his empty glove, both sides, and the boy looked at it with his mouth open, and Pallister tapped him on the end of the nose with one finger, and the penny was there, on the end of the boy's own nose, balanced, shining.
A sound went down the line. Not quite a laugh. The sound a crowd makes when it has been afraid and is told, for a moment, that it need not be.
Pallister took the penny off the boy's nose and put it in his hand and closed his fingers round it.
Then he dipped into the silver box, and took out a sweet.
Corin saw it. A small white thing, wrapped in a twist of paper. He knew the paper. He had taken one out of a bag of twenty vials under the Bourse on Sunday night, in a cellar, by the light of a stolen lamp. Care of the Dispensary, the Hill.
Pallister held it out.
The little boy took it.
And put his hand, with the sweet in it, into the pocket of his coat. Quickly. Deep down. And left it there. And looked back over his shoulder, down the three steps, at his mother.
Pallister watched him do it.
He did not stop smiling. He went on smiling at the little boy with his kind pink face and his gold spectacles, for a long moment, with the snow hissing in the braziers on either side of him. Then he looked past the boy. Down the steps. At the mother, at the bottom, with her hands twisted in her shawl. And past her, at the line. At the next child. And the next. At their hands. At all the hands, all down the Stairs, pushed down deep into pockets, and held there, and the mothers' hands on the shoulders above them, pressing.
Corin saw him see it.
And then Pallister bent forward again, toward the little boy, and said, in his soft dry warm voice, so gently that it hardly carried at all:
"Oh, no. Not in your pocket, my dear. It'll only melt in there, and stick to your penny." He smiled. "Eat it now. Here. For me. So I can see that you like it."
The little boy looked at him.
Then down at his mother.
His mother did not move.
"Go on," said Pallister, kindly. "It's peppermint. Your favorite. I can tell."
The little boy took his hand out of his pocket.
Corin, in the barrow, did not breathe.
The little boy unwrapped the twist of paper. Slowly. With small cold fingers. And looked at the white sweet on his palm. And at the kind old man. And put it in his mouth.
Pallister sat back in his chair.
"There," he said. "Good boy. Off you go. Next."
The little boy went down the three wooden steps with his cheek bulging and his penny in his fist, and his mother took him by the hand, and they went away across the fish hall floor between the empty tables, very fast, without looking back.
And the next child came up the steps.
A girl. Six, perhaps. With a hand in her pocket.
Corin lay in the bottom of the barrow under the gray blanket and watched it, and could not do anything. He could not get up. He could not walk. He could not shout. If he shouted, they would come to the barrow, and lift the blanket, and see his gray hands, and his face from the WANTED posters. And then there would be nobody at all.
He watched the girl come up to the chair.
He watched Pallister take her chin in his glove and turn her face to the light.
He watched him reach behind her ear for a penny.
And beside him, very low, so low it was hardly a breath, he heard the doctor say a word he had never heard Silas say before. And then another. And then Silas's long thin hand came down on the edge of the barrow and gripped it, so hard that the gray wood creaked.
"He knows," said Silas. "He saw the pockets. He knows somebody's warned them." His voice shook. "And now he'll make every one of them eat it in front of him. Two hundred. One at a time. And smile."
On the stage, the girl took the sweet.
And from halfway down the Stairs, in the middle of the line, somebody screamed.
Not a child. A woman. A great hoarse bellow of a scream, like a cow in a burning barn, that went up into the falling snow and out over the fish hall and the river and made the gulls on the roof go up all at once in a white screaming cloud.
"FEVER!"
Corin turned his head.
It was Bridie Kane. Standing on the Stairs with her bucket in one hand and the other arm flung out, pointing. Straight up the Stairs. Past the stage. Past the fish hall. At the corner of Fish Street, under the overhang of the chandler's shop.
At the barrow. And the white card tied to the end of it.
"FEVER!" bellowed Bridie Kane. "There's fever on the Stairs! The doctor's got a fever case, there, look, in the cart! Spotted fever! It's on the Stairs! It's in the line!"
